title: Email & password authentication with accounts-js and Apollo Server
body_markdown:
**[accounts-js](https://github.com/accounts-js/accounts) is a fullstack authentication and accounts-management for Javascript.** We provide you with a set of tools to authenticate and manage your users in your application. These tools work with REST, GraphQL and are database agnostic.


We will implement the Authentication GraphQL API in NodeJS using accounts-js and Apollo. At the end of this article, our server will be able to sign up new users, allow the users to login and authenticate them to protect some restricted information.


*At the end of this post, you can find a link to a repository containing the sources.*


### Requirements


For this project, you will need to have nodejs and mongodb installed on your system.


### Setup the node project


Let’s start by creating our NodeJS project. Create a new folder named` accounts-js-server` , all the project files should be inside this folder. Let’s initialize our new project using` npm` (you can use` yarn` if you prefer):


```text
npm init
```


Now, let’s add the dependencies we need to setup our Apollo GraphQL server.


```text
npm install apollo-server graphql
```


Create a new` index.js` file (to make this tutorial simpler all our code will be in a single file) and add this code to setup the Apollo server.


```text
1  // index.js    2    3  const    {   ApolloServer ,   gql  }    =    require  (  'apollo-server'  )  ;    4    5  const   typeDefs  =   gql `      6    type Query {     7      # This query will be protected so only authenticated users can access it     8      sensitiveInformation: String     9    }     10   `   ;    11    12  const   resolvers  =    {    13     Query  :    {    14       sensitiveInformation  :    (  )    =>    'Sensitive info'  ,    15     }  ,    16  }  ;    17    18  const   server  =    new    ApolloServer  (  {   typeDefs ,   resolvers  }  )  ;    19    20  // The `listen` method launches a web server.    21  server .  listen  (  )  .  then  (  (  {   url  }   )    =>    {    22    console .  log  (  `  🚀  Server ready at   ${  url }   `   )  ;    23  }  )  ;
```


Now let’s start the server to make sure everything is working as expected.


```text
node index.js
```


In your console you should see:


```text
🚀  Server ready at http://localhost:4000/
```


Our GraphQL server is now ready, it’s time to add accounts-js!


### Setup accounts-js


First, we will setup mongoose and connect to our database.


```text
npm install @accounts/mongo mongoose
```


```text
1  // index.js    2    3  const   mongoose  =    require  (  'mongoose'  )  ;    4  const    {   Mongo  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/mongo'  )  ;    5    6  // We connect mongoose to our local mongodb database    7  mongoose .  connect  (  'mongodb://localhost:27017/accounts-js-server'  ,    {    8     useNewUrlParser  :    true  ,    9     useUnifiedTopology  :    true  ,    10  }  )  ;    11    12  // We tell accounts-js to use the mongo connection    13  const   accountsMongo  =    new    Mongo  (  mongoose .  connection )  ;
```


Then, we add the accounts-js server dependencies.


```text
npm install @accounts/server @accounts/password
```


- ` @accounts/server` : The accounts-js core dependency.
- ` @accounts/password` : The accounts-js password service, it expose a set of function to manage and authenticate users using email + password.


It’s time to setup the accounts-js server configuration


```text
1  // index.js    2    3  const    {   AccountsServer  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/server'  )  ;    4  const    {   AccountsPassword  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/password'  )  ;    5    6  const   accountsPassword  =    new    AccountsPassword  (  {    7     // You can customise the behavior of the password service by providing some options    8  }  )  ;    9    10  const   accountsServer  =    new    AccountsServer  (    11     {    12       // We link the mongo adapter we created in the previous step to the server    13       db  :   accountsMongo ,    14       // Replace this value with a strong random secret    15       tokenSecret  :    'my-super-random-secret'  ,    16     }  ,    17     {    18       // We pass a list of services to the server, in this example we just use the password service    19       password  :   accountsPassword ,    20     }    21  )  ;
```


Then, we add the accounts-js graphql dependencies.


```text
npm install @accounts/graphql-api @graphql-toolkit/schema-merging @graphql-modules/core
```


- ` @accounts/graphql-api` : The transport layer exposing all the queries and mutations accounts-js provide.
- ` @graphql-toolkit/schema-merging` : Expose a set of tools that will help us to merge our schemas.
- ` @graphql-modules/core` : An internal dependency that accounts-js use to manage his graphql schema and resolvers.


Let’s merge the accounts-js GraphQL schema and our schema, so the user can access it


```text
1  // index.js    2    3  // Add makeExecutableSchema to the imported variables    4  const    {   ApolloServer ,   gql ,   makeExecutableSchema  }    =    require  (  'apollo-server'  )  ;    5  const    {   mergeTypeDefs ,   mergeResolvers  }    =    require  (  '@graphql-toolkit/schema-merging'  )  ;    6  const    {   AccountsModule  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/graphql-api'  )  ;    7    8  // We generate the accounts-js GraphQL module    9  const   accountsGraphQL  =   AccountsModule .  forRoot  (  {   accountsServer  }  )  ;    10    11  // A new schema is created combining our schema and the accounts-js schema    12  const   schema  =    makeExecutableSchema  (  {    13     typeDefs  :    mergeTypeDefs  (  [  typeDefs ,   accountsGraphQL .  typeDefs ]  )  ,    14     resolvers  :    mergeResolvers  (  [  accountsGraphQL .  resolvers ,   resolvers ]  )  ,    15     schemaDirectives  :    {    16       ...  accountsGraphQL .  schemaDirectives ,    17     }  ,    18  }  )  ;    19    20  // When we instantiate our Apollo server we use the schema and context properties    21  const   server  =    new    ApolloServer  (  {    22    schema ,    23     context  :   accountsGraphQL .  context ,    24  }  )  ;
```


At the end, our file should look like this:


```text
1  // index.js    2    3  const    {   ApolloServer ,   gql ,   makeExecutableSchema  }    =    require  (  'apollo-server'  )  ;    4  const   mongoose  =    require  (  'mongoose'  )  ;    5  const    {   Mongo  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/mongo'  )  ;    6  const    {   mergeTypeDefs ,   mergeResolvers  }    =    require  (  '@graphql-toolkit/schema-merging'  )  ;    7  const    {   AccountsServer  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/server'  )  ;    8  const    {   AccountsPassword  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/password'  )  ;    9  const    {   AccountsModule  }    =    require  (  '@accounts/graphql-api'  )  ;    10    11  // We connect mongoose to our local mongodb database    12  mongoose .  connect  (  'mongodb://localhost:27017/accounts-js-server'  ,    {    13     useNewUrlParser  :    true  ,    14     useUnifiedTopology  :    true  ,    15  }  )  ;    16    17  const   accountsMongo  =    new    Mongo  (  mongoose .  connection )  ;    18    19  const   typeDefs  =   gql `      20    type Query {     21      # This query will be protected so only authenticated users can access it     22      sensitiveInformation: String     23    }     24   `   ;    25    26  const   resolvers  =    {    27     Query  :    {    28       sensitiveInformation  :    (  )    =>    'Sensitive info'  ,    29     }  ,    30  }  ;    31    32  const   accountsPassword  =    new    AccountsPassword  (  {  }  )  ;    33    34  const   accountsServer  =    new    AccountsServer  (    35     {    36       db  :   accountsMongo ,    37       // Replace this value with a strong secret    38       tokenSecret  :    'my-super-random-secret'  ,    39     }  ,    40     {    41       password  :   accountsPassword ,    42     }    43  )  ;    44    45  // We generate the accounts-js GraphQL module    46  const   accountsGraphQL  =   AccountsModule .  forRoot  (  {   accountsServer  }  )  ;    47    48  // A new schema is created combining our schema and the accounts-js schema    49  const   schema  =    makeExecutableSchema  (  {    50     typeDefs  :    mergeTypeDefs  (  [  typeDefs ,   accountsGraphQL .  typeDefs ]  )  ,    51     resolvers  :    mergeResolvers  (  [  accountsGraphQL .  resolvers ,   resolvers ]  )  ,    52     schemaDirectives  :    {    53       ...  accountsGraphQL .  schemaDirectives ,    54     }  ,    55  }  )  ;    56    57  const   server  =    new    ApolloServer  (  {   schema ,    context  :   accountsGraphQL .  context  }  )  ;    58    59  // The `listen` method launches a web server.    60  server .  listen  (  )  .  then  (  (  {   url  }   )    =>    {    61    console .  log  (  `  🚀  Server ready at   ${  url }   `   )  ;    62  }  )  ;
```


If we restart our server and visit http://localhost:4000/, we should see that the accounts-js queries and mutations are merged with our schema. Our authentication server is now ready 🚀.


### Creating our first user


Inside the GraphQL Playground, let’s execute the following mutation:


```text
1  mutation    {    2     createUser  (    3       user  :    {    email  :    "john.doe@john.com"  ,    password  :    "superSecurePassword"    }    4     )    5  }
```


Congrats, our first user has been created 👏!


If you take a look at the` users` collection inside mongodb you should see that your user was created and looks like this:


```text
1  {    2     "_id"  :   ObjectId( "5e3da6ba13ef1a137bbc8fe4"  ) ,    3     "services"  :    {    4       "password"  :    {    5         "bcrypt"  :    "$2a$10$WwhjvbDzQpS2LrdkcgQJwODn.EE95T0b9NmMUNcHKyrDOlXEeybSq"    6       }    7     }  ,    8     "createdAt"  :    1581098682713  ,    9     "updatedAt"  :    1581098682713  ,    10     "emails"  :    [    11       {    12         "address"  :    "john.doe@john.com"  ,    13         "verified"  :    false    14       }    15     ]    16  }
```


What we can see is that a` createdAt` and` updatedAt` fields have been created. We also see that the password has been saved hashed in the database, we use bcrypt as a default but you can change it to argon2 via the options if you prefer.


Now let’s try to login with this user:


```text
1  mutation    {    2     authenticate  (    3       serviceName  :    " password  "    4       params  :    {    5         user  :    {    email  :    "john.doe@john.com"    }    6         password  :    "superSecurePassword"    7       }    8     )    {    9       sessionId    10       tokens    {    11         accessToken    12         refreshToken    13       }    14     }    15  }
```


You should see in the playground that a new session has been created. The session is represented by:


- a sessionId (you can check the session in the database)
- a short lived JWT accessToken used to authenticate the user
- a long lived refreshToken that can be used to get a new accessToken once it’s expired


Save the access token, we will need it to authenticate our requests in the next part.


### Protecting our query


Our first user has been created and we are now able to login via the API. Next step is to protect our` sensitiveInformation` query so only the authenticated users can access it.


accounts-js provide an` @auth` directive that we can use to protect our private queries.


Let’s add the directive to the query in our schema:


```text
1  // index.js    2    3  const   typeDefs  =   gql `      4    type Query {     5      # We add the @auth directive     6      sensitiveInformation: String @auth     7    }     8   `   ;
```


If you try this query, you should get an` Unauthorized` error 🛑. We can’t access this resource because we are not authenticated. To authenticate our request with the server we need to add the access token saved previously as a header of the request. The header key should be` authorization` and the value should be prefixed with` Bearer` . eg:` { "authorization": "Bearer my-access-token" }`


You made your first authenticated query, how cool is that?


Well, that’s it, you are done, you now have a Graphql server that can register and authenticate new users. Pretty simple right? Next step for you is to explore the playground and play with the different queries and mutations available (verify the email, change the password etc..) :).


You can find the source here[https://github.com/pradel/accounts-js-server-tutorial](https://github.com/pradel/accounts-js-server-tutorial) .


If you want to learn more about accounts-js head over our website and check the documentation[https://www.accountsjs.com/](https://www.accountsjs.com/) 🔐.
